metaDescription: Six plant caddies under $40 compared on pack size, four caster designs, 240 to 500 lb ratings and fit for one big pot or a whole collection of small ones.
introParagraphs: With this budget the most useful question is how many pots you actually move. A collection of small houseplants wants a multi pack where each base is cheap, while one monster planter wants a single caddy with a serious load rating. Choosing the wrong format means paying for capacity you do not need, or running short of bases.

We evaluated six distinct models: the Planterhoma six pack of 11.8 inch plastic dollies, the Lissomballon 12 inch wood pair, the Bamworld 12 inch wood pair, the WanderingDonkey 14 inch caddie, the Bosmere 16 inch with a 500 lb listed capacity and the VANCASTLE adjustable 15 to 22 inch frame. Color, size and pack variants of the same design, including a Bamworld four pack and a Bosmere 14 inch, are mentioned only as options.
The sections below compare them by pack count, caster layout, capacity and platform size, then explain what spending more would add.

products.name: Planterhoma 11.8 Inch Plastic Plant Caddy, 6 Pack
products.description:
The Planterhoma is a pack of six plastic dollies, each 11.8 inch across with four casters that rotate 360 degrees. The listing says two of the four wheels lock and that the casters tighten without tools. The plastic is described as heavy duty and well painted.

The case for this pack is arithmetic. If you have a row of medium pots, six bases cover them all, and four wheels per dolly spread each load wider than a pair of casters can. Two locks out of four is a sensible ratio for keeping a pot put. The listing does not give a load rating, so confirm it on the product page before putting a large planter on one.

In ownership, you will tighten twenty four casters, but with no tools needed it is quick work. At 11.8 inch the platform is slightly smaller than the 12 inch wood pairs, so very full pots may not sit flat. Compared with the Lissomballon pair at 240 lbs, you get three times as many bases but without a published rating.
products.bestFor: Collections of small to medium houseplants.
pros: Six bases cover a whole shelf of pots
Two of four casters lock on each
Plastic suits damp rooms and patios
cons: No load rating in the listing text

products.name: Bosmere 16 Inch Plant Caddie, 500 lb Capacity
products.description:
The Bosmere Down Under Plant Caddie is a single 16 inch roller with a listed 500 lb capacity. The listing says it works on pots of any shape and size and rolls on nylon and steel wheels, with one locking caster to hold it still.

It is the specialist for one big, heavy planter. A 500 lb rating is more than double the 240 lbs of the Lissomballon and well above the 265 lbs of the WanderingDonkey, so there is real headroom for stone or concrete. The single lock is the compromise, since it limits holding power on a slope.

In ownership, the 16 inch footprint suits wide terracotta and is kinder to heavy planters on a patio than a plastic dolly. A 14 inch Bosmere also exists at a similar spec, which fits smaller bases. Compared with the Planterhoma at 11.8 inch, you are buying one serious caddie in place of several light ones.
products.bestFor: One large, heavy planter on a deck or patio.
pros: 500 lb listed capacity is the top figure here
Nylon and steel wheels for outdoor surfaces

products.name: VANCASTLE Adjustable Plant Caddy, 15 to 22 Inch

specList.label: Capacity
specList.value: 450 lbs in title, 440 lbs in text

products.description:
The VANCASTLE is built from ABS panels and expandable stainless steel tubes, adjusting between 15 and 22 inch. The listing says the wheels lock and cites 450 lbs in the title and 440 lbs in a line of text, which we read as roughly that range.

It is the only pick that adapts to the pot. Square planters, rectangular troughs and wide bowls all fit by setting the frame width, and the 22 inch top end is beyond every fixed tray here. The listing compares its wheel favorably with a normal plastic single wheel.

In ownership, an adjustable frame needs a careful first setup and a check of each connection after a week. Compared with the Bosmere 16 inch, you gain range but lose a fixed, solid platform. Compared with the Planterhoma, one VANCASTLE costs more than several small dollies but carries far heavier planters.
products.bestFor: Square, rectangular or very wide planters.
cons: Two capacity figures in the listing
More parts to loosen over time

products.name: WanderingDonkey 14 Inch Plant Caddie
products.description:
The WanderingDonkey is a one piece plastic caddie, 14.17 inch outside and 12.68 inch inside, rated for 265 lbs. The listing describes toughened tempered plastic, a frosted surface and no assembly, and says it rolls on hardwood, concrete and carpet.

It is the middle option on size and capacity, above the 12 inch pairs and below the Bosmere. The no assembly design means there is nothing to tighten. The listing does not mention wheel locks and the saucer has no drain holes, so it suits pots that you water elsewhere on a level floor.

In ownership, it is the easy button for one mid weight pot. Compared with the Planterhoma it is one base instead of six, and it states a load rating where the Planterhoma does not. Compared with the Bosmere it gives up 235 lbs of rating and a locking caster. The frosted finish is a cosmetic point rather than a performance one, so weigh the rating and the lack of locks instead.
products.bestFor: One mid weight pot on a level floor, no setup.
pros: Rolls on hardwood, concrete and carpet
Wider base than the 12 inch pairs
cons: No drain holes in the saucer

products.name: Lissomballon 12 Inch Wood Plant Caddy, 2 Pack
products.description:
The Lissomballon is a pair of 12 inch round wood caddies with 360 degree lockable casters and a stated 240 lbs rating. The frame is described as carbon wood, and the listing mentions uses beyond plants, such as laundry bins and trash cans.

It is the best value for two indoor pots. You get a stated load rating, locks on the casters and a natural look. The platform is only 12 inch, so wider pots are out, and the wood should always sit under a saucer.

In ownership, two lightweight bases are easy to store and rotate. Compared with the Planterhoma six pack, you get fewer bases but a published rating, and compared with the Bosmere you get far lower capacity but more locks. If you want four matching bases later, the Bamworld pack sizes are easier to extend than a single pair.
products.bestFor: Two indoor pots of medium weight.

products.name: Bamworld 12 Inch Plant Caddy, 2 Pack
products.description:
The Bamworld is a pair of 12 inch round wood trays with metal connections and casters that the listing says lock. It is sold in other pack sizes too, including a four pack, which is useful if you have more pots to move. The listing describes premium wood and smooth rolling.

This is the look first option for living rooms and the one to scale up if you want matching bases for four plants. The listing does not state a load rating, so check the product page before loading it. For a stated number, use the Lissomballon at 240 lbs.

In ownership, keep the wood dry and use a saucer. Compared with the plastic Planterhoma, it looks better in a room but gives less certainty about weight.
products.bestFor: Matching bases in a visible indoor spot.
cons: No load rating in the listing

buyingCriteria.criterion: Pack size versus per base cost
buyingCriteria.explanation: A multi pack lowers the cost per base but spreads quality thin. The Planterhoma gives six bases in one pack, the Lissomballon and Bamworld give two, and the Bosmere, VANCASTLE and WanderingDonkey are single units. If you have six houseplants, six bases keeps them all mobile. If you have one monster planter, a single high rated base beats six small ones. Mixing is allowed, since nothing stops you buying a pack for the small pots and one heavy single for the biggest planter. A pack also leaves a spare base for the next repot.

More casters spread the load, and more locks hold it. The Planterhoma has four casters per dolly with two locking, the Lissomballon and Bamworld list lockable casters and the Bosmere lists one locking caster. A four wheel base resists tipping when pushed across a threshold. Two locks of four is a better holding ratio than one lock of a few. Four wheels also let a dolly roll straight when one wheel meets a gap, which a two wheel base does not do as well.

A rating is only useful if it exists. The Lissomballon states 240 lbs, the WanderingDonkey 265 lbs, the VANCASTLE roughly 440 to 450 lbs and the Bosmere 500 lb, while the Planterhoma and Bamworld listings give none. Estimate the wet pot weight and keep a 20 percent margin. When in doubt, buy the stated rating over the unstated one. A pack of six with an unstated rating can still suit pots you can lift with one hand, since a light pot never approaches a limit.

The pot base should sit fully on the platform. The Planterhoma is 11.8 inch, the wood pairs are 12 inch, the WanderingDonkey is 12.68 inch inside, the Bosmere is 16 inch and the VANCASTLE reaches 22 inch. A pot with flared sides may have a much smaller base than its rim suggests, so measure at the bottom. Leave about an inch of clearance on all sides, so the pot does not rock on its edge. The Planterhoma's 11.8 inch size is a quarter inch under the 12 inch pairs, so check tight fits.

Plastic and ABS tolerate damp rooms and patios, wood belongs indoors with a saucer, and nylon with steel suits rough ground. The Planterhoma is plastic, the Lissomballon and Bamworld are wood and the Bosmere uses nylon and steel wheels. Pick by where the pot lives, not only by what looks good. Padding such as felt under a plastic or wood caddy protects finished floors from scratches. Check floors under outdoor caddies for rust marks from metal parts.

Past this cap, you can expect more wheels per base, bigger platforms and stronger frames, as well as sets with matched saucers. The Bosmere already offers the highest rating here, so the step up is about extra locks and size beyond 22 inch. Pay for it only if your pots stay beyond what the VANCASTLE can span. Larger sets with matched saucers and rims, and bases with four locking wheels, sit above this budget.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pack value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared what you get per purchase, from the six base Planterhoma to single units like the Bosmere. We weighed how many pots a typical household moves. A pack was valued only when each base was usable on its own. We considered storage too, since six bases need room when the plants are not on them.

howWeEvaluated.title: Wheel layout and locks
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted casters and locks, including the Planterhoma's four casters with two locks and the Bosmere's single lock. Layout affects stability on thresholds. Models that do not state locks were scored accordingly. Wheels were judged on count and locks first and material second.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity clarity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated ratings from 240 lbs to 500 lb and noted listings that give none. The VANCASTLE's two figures were treated as a range. A stated number beat an unstated one. We also weighed the gap between 240 lbs and 500 lb as the difference between a medium houseplant and a large floor planter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and adjustability
howWeEvaluated.description: Platforms range from 11.8 inch to an adjustable 22 inch. We matched sizes to common pots and flagged risk of overhang. The VANCASTLE scored highest for flexibility. We flagged the Planterhoma at 11.8 inch as the smallest platform in the lineup.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value inside the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Six models sit under the cap, covering packs, singles and an adjustable frame. We weighed each against what it gives up. Positioning comes from listing specs and buyer feedback, not hands on measurement. We asked whether each pick solves a specific job, such as a collection, a heavy pot or an odd shaped pot.

faq.q: Which plant caddy under this budget is best?
faq.a: It depends on pot count. The Planterhoma six pack is best for many small pots, the Bosmere is best for one heavy planter and the VANCASTLE is best for wide or square ones. The Lissomballon pair is the best rated indoor pair.

faq.q: How many pots can I roll with the Planterhoma?
faq.a: The pack contains six dollies, so up to six pots. The listing says each has four casters with two locking. Check the product page for the load rating, since the listing text does not give one.

faq.q: Is a bigger weight rating always better?
faq.a: Only if you need it. A 500 lb Bosmere is wasted under a small houseplant, and a heavy base is harder to move. Match the rating to the wet pot weight with a 20 percent margin.
On slopes and near doors, yes. The Planterhoma, Lissomballon, Bamworld and VANCASTLE list locks, while the WanderingDonkey does not. The Bosmere lists one locking caster.

faq.q: Can I use wood caddies on a patio?
faq.a: Only on a covered one. Wood swells with standing water, so use a saucer. Plastic or nylon models handle rain better.

faq.q: How do I fit an odd shaped pot?
faq.a: Measure the base, not the rim. A square or oval pot is best on the adjustable VANCASTLE. A round caddy under a square pot leaves corners unsupported.

faq.q: Why might cheap caddy wheels fail?
faq.a: Buyers sometimes report wheels that loosen or detach under load. Tighten the casters at setup and recheck after a week. Keep the load well under the rating.
